     The lighthouse stood on a knuckle of black rock that the sea had been
     trying to swallow since before there were maps to name it. Three hundred
     and eleven steps spiraled up its spine, each one worn into a shallow bowl
     by the boots of keepers who had come before him. Elias knew every step by
     heart. He knew the seventh one that always groaned, the two hundredth
     that caught the heel, the final turn where the wind found the gap in the
     glass and sang a thin, silver note.

     His wife, Maren, had come to the light as a bride, carrying a trunk of
     books and a stubborn belief that the sea was beautiful. She had been
     right, and she had been wrong, and she had stayed anyway. When the fever
     took her in the winter of his nineteenth year as keeper, Elias stopped
     speaking to the village. He spoke to the lamp instead.
